title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 68 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 443–444 (Night 68, continuing directly from nights-67), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 68 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The king's letter to Sharkān tells how, returning from a month's hunting, he found his son and daughter gone on the pilgrimage, and ends in a lament in verse; Sharkān reads it, grieves and rejoices in the same breath, and goes in to his wife Nuzhat al-Zamān, who bears a daughter. When he sees the bead at the baby's neck he recognises it, demands where she got it, and is told the truth: she is his sister. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-sittūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the sixty,
sentences.i: And when it was the sixty-eighth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَ عُمَرَ بْنَ النُّعْمَانِ قَالَ فِي مَكْتُوبِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika ʿUmara ibna al-Nuʿmāni qāla fī maktūbihi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that King ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān said in his letter:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān wrote in his letter:
sentences.n: The print runs السعيد and أن together (al-saʿīdu anna); kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنْصِ غِبْتُ شَهْرًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dhahabtu ilā al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanṣi ghibtu shahran
sentences.l: And when I went to the hunting and the sport-of-the-chase, I was away a month.
sentences.i: When I went out to hunt and to chase game, I was away a month.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَتَيْتُ وَجَدْتُ أَخَاكَ وَأُخْتَكَ أَخَذَا شَيْأً مِنَ الْمَالِ وَسَافَرَا مَعَ الْحُجَّاجِ إِلَى الْحَجِّ خُفْيَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ataytu wajadtu akhāka wa-ukhtaka akhadhā shayʾan mina al-māli wa-sāfarā maʿa al-ḥujjāji ilā al-ḥajji khufyatan
sentences.l: And when I came, I found your brother and your sister had taken something of the money and travelled with the pilgrims to the pilgrimage, secretly.
sentences.i: When I came back, I found that your brother and your sister had taken some of the money and set out secretly with the pilgrims for the pilgrimage.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَلِمْتُ بِذَلِكَ ضَاقَ بِيَ الْفَضَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿalimtu bi-dhālika ḍāqa bī al-faḍāʾu
sentences.l: And when I knew of that, the open-space grew narrow upon me.
sentences.i: When I learned of it, the wide world grew narrow for me.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي يَا وَلَدِي قَدِ انْتَظَرْتُ مَجِيءَ الْحُجَّاجِ لَعَلَّهُمَا يَجِيئَانِ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-innī yā waladī qadi intaẓartu majīʾa al-ḥujjāji laʿallahumā yajīʾāni maʿahum
sentences.l: And I, O my son, have waited for the coming of the pilgrims, that perhaps the two of them would come with them.
sentences.i: And I, my son, waited for the pilgrims to return, hoping that the two of them might come back with them.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ الْحُجَّاجُ سَائَتُ عَنْهُمَا فَمَا أَخْبَرَنِي عَنْهُمَا أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa al-ḥujjāju saʾatu ʿanhumā fa-mā akhbaranī ʿanhumā aḥadun
sentences.l: And when the pilgrims came, I asked about the two of them, and no one told me anything about the two of them.
sentences.i: When the pilgrims came, I asked after the two of them, and no one could tell me anything of them.
sentences.n: The print has سائت where the sense is سألت (saʾaltu, “I asked”); the compositor seems to have dropped the lām. The letters are kept as printed and vocalized as they stand.

sentences.t: فَلَبِسْتُ لِأَجْلِهِمَا ثِيَابَ الْحُزْنِ وَأَنَا مَرْهُونُ الْفُؤَادِ عَلِيمُ الرَّقَادِ غَرِيقُ دَمْعِ الْعَيْنِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-labistu li-ajlihimā thiyāba al-ḥuzni wa-anā marhūnu al-fuʾādi ʿalīmu al-raqādi gharīqu damʿi al-ʿayni wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: So I put on, for the sake of the two of them, the garments of grief, and I am pledged-of-heart, knowing-of-sleep, drowned-in the tear of the eye; and he recited, saying:
sentences.i: So for their sake I put on the garments of mourning, my heart held in pawn, sleep a stranger to me, my eyes drowned in tears; and he recited, saying:
sentences.n: عليم الرقاد (“knowing of sleep”) is as printed and gives poor sense; عديم الرقاد (“without sleep”) is the likely intended reading, which is what the idiomatic line follows. The writer then breaks into the first-person “I” and back to “he recited”, a shift the text itself makes.

sentences.t:
خَيَالُهُمَا مَا لَيْسَ يَبْرَحُ سَاعَةً * جَعَلْتُ لَهُ فِي الْقَلْبِ أَشْرَفَ مَوْضِعِ
وَلَوْلَارَجَاءُ الْعَوْدِ مَاعِشْتُ سَاعَةً * وَلَوْلَا خَيَالُ الطَّيْفِ لَمْ أَتَهَجَّعِ
sentences.tr:
khayāluhumā mā laysa yabraḥu sāʿatan * jaʿaltu lahu fī al-qalbi ashrafa mawḍiʿi
wa-lawlā rajāʾu al-ʿawdi mā ʿishtu sāʿatan * wa-lawlā khayālu al-ṭayfi lam atahajjaʿi
sentences.l:
Their image — which does not leave for an hour — I have set for it in the heart the noblest place.
And were it not for hope of return, I would not have lived an hour; and were it not for the phantom of the visitor-in-the-night, I would not have slept a little.
sentences.i:
Their image never leaves me for an hour; I have given it the noblest place in my heart.
Were it not for hope of their return I could not have lived an hour, and were it not for the phantom that visits in the night, I could not have slept at all.
sentences.n: Verse copied exactly as the edition prints it, marks and all. In the second line the print joins ولولا to رجاء (wa-lawlā rajāʾ) and ما to عشت (mā ʿishtu); kept as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَ مِنْ جُمْلَةِ الْمَكْتُوبِ وَبَعْدَ السَّلَامِ عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَى مَنْ عِنْدَكَ أُعَرِّفُكَ أَنَّكَ لَاتَتَهَاوَنْ فِي كَشْفِ الْأَخْبَارِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا عَلَيْنَا عَارٌ
sentences.tr: thumma kataba min jumlati al-maktūbi wa-baʿda al-salāmi ʿalayka wa-ʿalā man ʿindaka uʿarrifuka annaka lātatahāwan fī kashfi al-akhbāri fa-inna hādhā ʿalaynā ʿārun
sentences.l: Then he wrote, among the sum of the writing: And after peace upon you and upon whoever is with you, I let you know that you must-not-be-lax in the uncovering of the reports, for this is, upon us, a shame.
sentences.i: Then he wrote, among the rest of the letter: After greeting you and all who are with you, I tell you not to be slack in seeking out news of them, for this is a disgrace to us.
sentences.n: The print writes لاتتهاون as one word; kept as printed. It is read here as a prohibition (“do not be lax”), which suits the sense.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأَ الْكِتَابَ حَزِنَ عَلَى أَبِيهِ وَفَرِحَ لِفَقْدِ أُخْتِهِ وَأَخِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾa al-kitāba ḥazina ʿalā abīhi wa-fariḥa li-faqdi ukhtihi wa-akhīhi
sentences.l: And when he read the letter, he grieved over his father and was glad at the loss of his sister and his brother.
sentences.i: When Sharkān read the letter, he grieved for his father, yet was glad of the loss of his sister and his brother.
sentences.n: A bitter touch: Sharkān, the eldest son, stands to be sole heir if the other two are never found.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ الْكِتَابَ وَدَخَلَ بِهِ عَلَى زَوْجَتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَنَّهَا أُخْتُهُ وَهِيَ لَا تَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ أَخُوهَا مَعَ أَنَّهُ يَتَرَدَّدُ عَلَيْهَا لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا إِلَى أَنْ كَمَلَتْ أَشْهُرُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha al-kitāba wa-dakhala bihi ʿalā zawjatihi Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-lam yaʿlam annahā ukhtuhu wa-hiya lā taʿlamu annahu akhūhā maʿa annahu yataraddadu ʿalayhā laylan wa-nahāran ilā an kamalat ashhuruhā
sentences.l: And he took the letter and went in with it to his wife Nuzhat al-Zamān, not knowing that she was his sister, and she not knowing that he was her brother, though he went-back-and-forth to her night and day, until her months were complete.
sentences.i: He took the letter and went in with it to his wife, Nuzhat al-Zamān. He did not know that she was his sister, nor she that he was her brother, though he came to her night and day until her months were complete.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّ الطَّلْقِ فَسَهَّلَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهَا الْوِلَادَةَ فَوَلَدَتْ بِنْتًا
sentences.tr: wa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyi al-ṭalqi fa-sahhala Allāhu ʿalayhā al-wilādata fa-waladat bintan
sentences.l: And she sat upon the chair of the labour-pangs, and God made the birthing easy for her, and she bore a girl.
sentences.i: She sat on the birthing chair, and God made the delivery easy for her, and she bore a daughter.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلَتْ تَطْلُبُ شَرْكَانَ فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ قَالَتْ لَهُ هَذِهِ بِنْتُكَ فَسَمِّهَا مَا تُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-arsalat taṭlubu Sharkāna fa-lammā raʾathu qālat lahu hādhihi bintuka fa-sammihā mā turīdu
sentences.l: And she sent, seeking Sharkān; and when she saw him, she said to him: This is your daughter, so name her what you wish.
sentences.i: She sent for Sharkān, and when she saw him she said, “This is your daughter. Name her whatever you wish.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَادَةُ النَّاسِ أَنْ يُسَمُّوا أَوْلَادَهُمْ فِي سَابِعِ يَوْمِ وِلَادَتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿādatu al-nāsi an yusammū awlādahum fī sābiʿi yawmi wilādatihim
sentences.l: And he said: The custom of the people is that they name their children on the seventh day of their birth.
sentences.i: He said, “It is the custom of people to name their children on the seventh day after birth.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ انْحَنَى شَرْكَانُ عَلَى ابْنَتِهِ وَقَبَّلَهَا فَوَجَدَ فِي عُنُقِهَاخَرَزَةً مُعَلَّقَةً مِنَ الثَّلَٰثِ خَرَزَاتٍ الَّتِي جَاءَتْ بِهَا الْمَلِكُ أَبْرِيزَةُ مِنْ بِلَادِ الرُّومِ
sentences.tr: thumma inḥanā Sharkānu ʿalā ibnatihi wa-qabbalahā fa-wajada fī ʿunuqihākharazatan muʿallaqatan mina al-thalāthi kharazātin allatī jāʾat bihā al-maliku Abrīzatu min bilādi al-Rūmi
sentences.l: Then Sharkān bent over his daughter and kissed her, and found on her neck a bead hung — of the three beads which the king Abrīza brought from the lands of Rūm.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān bent over his daughter and kissed her, and found a bead hanging at her neck, one of the three beads that Abrīza had brought from the land of Rūm.
sentences.n: Two printer's slips: عنقها and خرزة are run together (ʿunuqihā-kharazatan), and الثلث stands for الثلاث (“the three”), pointed with the dagger alif. Abrīza is a woman and the verb is feminine (jāʾat), yet the print says الملك, “the king”; kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَايَنَ الْخَرَزَةَ مُعَلَّقَةً فِي عُنُقِ ابْنَتِهِ غَابَ عَقْلُهُ وَلَحِقَهُ الْغَيْظُ وَحَمْلَقَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَعَرَفَ الْخَرَزَةَ حَقَّ مَعْرِفَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿāyana al-kharazata muʿallaqatan fī ʿunuqi ibnatihi ghāba ʿaqluhu wa-laḥiqahu al-ghayẓu wa-ḥamlaqa ʿaynayhi wa-ʿarafa al-kharazata ḥaqqa maʿrifatihā
sentences.l: And when he beheld the bead hung on the neck of his daughter, his mind went-away, and rage overtook him, and he stared-wide with his eyes, and he knew the bead the true-right of its knowing.
sentences.i: When he saw the bead hanging at his daughter’s neck, his wits left him and rage seized him; he stared wide-eyed, for he knew that bead beyond all doubt.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ إِلَى نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَٰلَ لَهَا مِنْ أَيْنَ جَائَتْكِ هَذِهِ الْخَرَزَةُ يَاجَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara ilā Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-qāla lahā min ayna jāʾatki hādhihi al-kharazatu yājāriyatu
sentences.l: Then he looked at Nuzhat al-Zamān and said to her: From where came to you this bead, O slave-girl?
sentences.i: Then he looked at Nuzhat al-Zamān and said to her, “Where did you get this bead, slave-girl?”
sentences.n: The print has قل for قال (dagger alif), and joins يا to جارية (yājāriyatu). Sharkān still calls his wife by the title of a slave girl, which is what stings her in the next sentence.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مِنْ شَرْكَانَ ذَٰلِكَ الْكَلَامَ قَالَتْ لَهُ أَنَا سَيِّدَتُكَ وَسَيِّدَةُ كُلِّ مَنْ فِي قَصْرِكَ أَمَا تَسْتَحِي وَأَنْتَ تَقُولُ يَا جَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat min Sharkāna dhālika al-kalāma qālat lahu anā sayyidatuka wa-sayyidatu kulli man fī qaṣrika amā tastaḥī wa-anta taqūlu yā jāriyatu
sentences.l: And when she heard that speech from Sharkān, she said to him: I am your mistress and the mistress of everyone in your palace. Are you not ashamed, when you say “O slave-girl”?
sentences.i: When she heard those words from Sharkān, she said to him, “I am your mistress, and the mistress of everyone in your palace. Have you no shame, calling me ‘slave-girl’?

sentences.t: أَنَا مَلِكَةٌ بِنْتُ مَلِكٍ وَالْآنَ زَالَ الْكِتْمَانُ وَاشْتَهَرَ الْأَمْرُ وَبَانَ أَنَا نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ بِنْتُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: anā malikatun bintu malikin wa-al-āna zāla al-kitmānu wa-ishtahara al-amru wa-bāna anā Nuzhatu al-Zamāni bintu al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni
sentences.l: I am a queen, daughter of a king; and now the concealment has gone, and the matter has become known, and it has appeared: I am Nuzhat al-Zamān, daughter of King ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān.
sentences.i: I am a queen, the daughter of a king. Now the secret is gone and the matter is out: I am Nuzhat al-Zamān, daughter of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān.”
sentences.n: Her speech continues from the previous sentence, hence no opening quotation mark here. وبان أنا (“it appeared: I am”) lacks the usual anna after bāna; kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنْهَا هَذَا الْكَلَامَ لَحِقَهُ الِارْتِعَاشُ وَأَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa minhā hādhā al-kalāma laḥiqahu al-irtiʿāshu wa-aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi
sentences.l: And when he heard from her this speech, trembling overtook him, and he bowed with his head to the ground.
sentences.i: When he heard these words from her, a trembling seized him, and he bowed his head to the ground.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُ—بَ—احِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The stock close of a night. The print's last word is damaged (الم—ب—اح, with dashes inside it); it is read as the formula's usual al-mubāḥ.
